questions.sectionHeading: Section II (80 marks). Attempt Questions 21–34. Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.
questions.stem: Compare eras and periods in the Geological Time Scale. Your response should include TWO similarities or differences with reference to examples.

criteria.text: Identifies similarities or differences ; Supports similarities or differences with examples
Identifies similarities or differences ; OR ; Identifies one similarity or difference and supports with an example
Identifies one feature of an era or period ; OR ; Names an era or period correctly

questions.sampleAnswer:
Eras are longer than periods, for example, the Cenozoic Era covers more than 60 Ma but the Quaternary Period only covers about 2 Ma.
Eras and Periods are both defined by major changes in evolution, for example, the Palaeozoic Era and Cambrian Period were both marked by the first appearance of hard-shelled animals.

questions.stem: Assess the role of blue carbon ecosystems in reducing the rate of global warming.
questions.stimulus: Blue carbon ecosystems such as saltmarshes, mangroves and seagrass forests can store 10 times more carbon in their soil than temperate forests, and 50 times more than rainforests. Most of the carbon in blue carbon ecosystems is stored in the soils rather than in the plants.

criteria.text: Explains how an increased capacity to capture carbon can reduce amount of carbon entering the atmosphere ; Links atmospheric carbon to global warming ; Makes a judgement of value of blue carbon ecosystems in terms of their role in slowing global warming
Describes the role of carbon sinks in regulating carbon content in the atmosphere ; Links role of carbon to global warming ; Implies a judgement
Outlines one feature of blue carbon ecosystems that makes them a better carbon sink than terrestrial ecosystems ; OR ; Outlines how blue carbon ecosystems act as a carbon sink
Provides some relevant information

questions.sampleAnswer: Blue carbon ecosystems are very important as they are able to store large amounts of carbon in their soils. This ability to store carbon in the soil prevents large amounts of carbon dioxide from entering the atmosphere, effectively slowing the rate of global warming as the carbon dioxide present in the atmosphere traps heat causing global warming.

questions.stimulus:

[Diagram, with KEY: a sun at the top left; a hollow arrow labelled Sunlight in the KEY pointing down to a grey curved surface; filled grey circles (labelled Greenhouse gas in the KEY) and open circles (labelled Other gas) scattered in the space above the surface; a clock symbol (labelled Time passing in the KEY) on the surface; thin arrows (labelled Infrared radiation in the KEY) leaving the surface: one long arrow to the upper left, two arrows rising to the upper right, and a cluster of short arrows around one filled grey circle.]

criteria.text: Explains the greenhouse effect ; Refers to the model in explanation including the role of greenhouse gases and infrared radiation
Describes the greenhouse effect ; Refers to the model including the role of greenhouse gases and infrared radiation

questions.sampleAnswer: Sunlight, shown by the large arrow, is absorbed by the surface of the Earth, heating the Earth. The clock shows that some heat is later radiated away from the Earth in the form of infrared radiation. Some of this heat is trapped within the atmosphere as it strikes a greenhouse gas molecule and is scattered back through the atmosphere as shown by the short arrows in the model. This keeps the Earth and its atmosphere warm.

questions.stem: Explain why high magnitude earthquakes such as the 2021 Mansfield earthquake are rare on mainland Australia.
questions.stimulus:
The following source contains information from an item published in ABC News online on 22 September 2021.
Source: an extract from ABC News online, 'Mansfield magnitude-5.9 earthquake shakes Melbourne, regional Victoria, southern NSW, Sydney, Canberra, Adelaide and Launceston', 22 September 2021. The extract is copyright and is not reproduced here; read it in the 2022 HSC Earth and Environmental Science paper (Question 27, page 20): https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/noindex/2025-05/2022-hsc-earth-and-environmental-science.pdf
[Summary of what the item reports: Geoscience Australia detected the earthquake at about 9:15 am in the Alpine National Park south-east of Mansfield, Victoria, at a depth of 10 kilometres; it was one of the largest earthquakes in eastern Australia since European settlement; a photograph shows part of a building in Chapel Street, Melbourne, that crumbled; there were 100 requests for assistance, about 55 in metropolitan Melbourne, and most of the minor structural damage was to chimneys and facades; a spokesperson said it was fortunate the epicentre was in a less populated regional area.]

questions.sampleAnswer: High magnitude earthquakes usually occur on tectonic plate boundaries as the plates move relative to one another. There are no tectonic plate boundaries within the Australian continent, so high magnitude earthquakes are rare.

questions.stimulus:
The following source contains information from an item published in ABC News online on 22 September 2021.
Source: an extract from ABC News online, 'Mansfield magnitude-5.9 earthquake shakes Melbourne, regional Victoria, southern NSW, Sydney, Canberra, Adelaide and Launceston', 22 September 2021. The extract is copyright and is not reproduced here; read it in the 2022 HSC Earth and Environmental Science paper (Question 27, page 20): https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/noindex/2025-05/2022-hsc-earth-and-environmental-science.pdf
[Summary of what the item reports: Geoscience Australia detected the earthquake at about 9:15 am in the Alpine National Park south-east of Mansfield, Victoria, at a depth of 10 kilometres; it was one of the largest earthquakes in eastern Australia since European settlement; a photograph shows part of a building in Chapel Street, Melbourne, that crumbled; there were 100 requests for assistance, about 55 in metropolitan Melbourne, and most of the minor structural damage was to chimneys and facades; a spokesperson said it was fortunate the epicentre was in a less populated regional area.]

criteria.text: Describes the effects of earthquakes on the biosphere and built environment ; Makes a judgement as to the extent of effects on the biosphere and built environment
Outlines the effects of earthquakes on the biosphere and built environment ; Makes a judgement as to the extent of effects on the biosphere or built environment
Outlines the effects of earthquakes on the biosphere or built environment
Provides some relevant information

questions.sampleAnswer:
Earthquakes cause the ground to shake. Most trees and plants can withstand some movement so they are rarely damaged. Animals may, in rare cases, be hit by falling branches. Microorganisms are usually unaffected. Earthquakes such as the 2021 Mansfield earthquake generally have little effect on the biosphere.
Australian earthquakes are rare and weak, so the Australian built environment contains rigid structures that are often not designed to withstand movement. Brick structures can crack. Power lines can fall. Earthquakes such as the 2021 Mansfield earthquake have the potential to cause major damage if they occur under built environments.

questions.sectionHeading: Section II (80 marks). Attempt Questions 21–34. Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.
questions.stem: Design a valid procedure to test the student’s hypothesis. Your response should include a method for changing the independent variable, measurement of independent and dependent variables, management of controlled variables, use of a control and appropriate safe work practices.
questions.stimulus:
A student wanted to investigate the effect of photosynthesising cyanobacteria on the oxygenation of the atmosphere. The student developed the following hypothesis:
Increasing light levels enables photosynthesising cyanobacteria to produce greater quantities of oxygen.
The student was provided with the following equipment:
• 10 g living cyanobacteria culture (can be separated)
• 10 light-proof cupboards
• 10 lamps with variable brightness
• 10 remote sensing light meters
• 10 sets of glassware and water as shown in the following diagram
• spatula
• laboratory balance/scales
• water.
[Diagram of labelled apparatus: a graduated measuring cylinder, its upper part holding trapped oxygen, with its lower end extending into a filter funnel; the funnel sits in a beaker of water; oxygen bubbles rise through the funnel and cylinder; a grey mound labelled cyanobacteria culture lies in the bottom of the funnel. Labels: Trapped oxygen; Oxygen bubbles; Measuring cylinder; Beaker; Filter funnel; Water; Cyanobacteria culture.]

criteria.text: Identifies variables explicitly or implicitly ; Describes all of the requirements for a valid procedure ; Provides a clear and logical sequence
Outlines most of the requirements for a valid procedure ; Provides a clear and logical sequence
Outlines some of the requirements for a valid procedure
Identifies some aspects of relevant experimental procedure
Identifies one aspect of relevant experimental procedure

questions.sampleAnswer:
Separate the cyanobacteria into ten equal samples. Place each sample under a funnel as shown in the diagram, ensuring no air is trapped in the measuring cylinder. Number the beakers 1−10.
Changing and measuring the independent variable (light)
Place each sample in a lightproof cupboard. Beaker 1 (the control) should be left in the dark. Illuminate samples 2−10 with a lamp. Set lamp 2 to minimum brightness and set lamps 3−10 progressively brighter with lamp 10 set to maximum. Use a light meter in each cupboard to measure light levels throughout the experiment.
Managing controlled variables
Weigh each cyanobacteria sample to exactly one gram. Use markings on the beakers to ensure each sample has the same quantity of water. Use cupboards in the same room to ensure consistent temperature. Give each sample the same time to photosynthesise between set-up and oxygen measurement.
Measuring the dependent variable (oxygen production)
Measure the displaced water level in each measuring cylinder after one week to show oxygen production.
Safety
Clean water spills promptly to avoid slips and falls. Take care with glass to avoid breakages and cuts.

questions.sampleAnswer: Bushfires burn large areas of vegetation. questions.stimulus: [Three greyscale photographs in a row, each with a caption. Left: 'Stromatolites', a rocky, mound-shaped formation in shallow water. Middle: 'Modern plants', a rose flower with leaves. Right: 'Modern animals', two kangaroos on grass.]

questions.sampleAnswer: Organic molecules found around black smokers in the ancient oceans organised themselves into simple cells which were able to obtain energy using chemicals emitted by the black smokers. Over time these cells evolved into photosynthesising cyanobacteria which can be found within ancient stromatolites. The development of hard body parts in organisms such as the Cambrian trilobites provided protection and greater mobility allowing fauna such as the labyrinthodont to move into terrestrial environments. This allowed the Earth’s biosphere to diversify as fauna inhabited a whole range of new and different ecosystems, eventually creating our present biosphere.
